cards.explanation: The answer is that Joab demands to know why David let Abner go. Joab walks in and asks the king, “What have you done?” Then he asks why David dismissed Abner, since Abner is getting away. I bet David was hoping for a warmer welcome home for Joab's men.

The answer is that Joab says Abner came to deceive David and track his movements. Joab says Abner “…came to deceive you and to track your movements and all that you are doing.” That's Joab's charge against Abner, friends. Joab makes the accusation, and then he sends messengers after Abner.

The answer is True. Right after Joab leaves David, he sends messengers after Abner, and the text says, “But David was unaware of it.” The king stayed in the dark while all of this was happening, friends. That's one big thing happening behind a closed door.

The answer is that Joab makes it look as if he wants to talk privately. He pulled Abner aside into the gateway “…as if to speak to him privately…” It looked like a quiet word between two men. This is one of the heavy parts of the story, friends, and I think it lands hard.

The word is guiltless. David says, “I and my kingdom are forever guiltless before the LORD concerning the blood of Abner son of Ner.” He says it right when he hears the news, friends. He makes clear whose hands did this, and they weren't his.

The answer is False. David doesn't ask for forgiveness here. He says, “May it whirl over the head of Joab and over the entire house of his father…” He goes on to name hard things he wants for that house, and I think this one's heavy to read.

The answer is in the battle at Gibeon. The text says Joab and his brother Abishai murdered Abner because he had killed their brother Asahel “…in the battle at Gibeon.” So this whole thing traces back to a battle, friends. I think that's the weight behind the verse about Asahel's blood.

The answer is that David orders them to tear their clothes and mourn Abner. He orders Joab and all the people with him, “Tear your clothes, put on sackcloth, and mourn before Abner.” Notice that Joab is included in that order, friends. David puts everyone in mourning for Abner.
The answer is True. The text says, “…King David himself walked behind the funeral bier.” He walked right behind Abner, friends. A king doesn't have to do that, so I think it says something.

The answer is that David weeps aloud. The text says the king “…wept aloud at Abner’s tomb…” and all the people wept too. No holding it in, friends. The next thing the king does is sing a lament (2 Samuel 3:33).

The answer is that all the people weep over Abner even more. The text says, “…all the people wept over him even more.” That comes right after David's lament for Abner, friends. I bet it was a long, heavy day in Hebron.

The answer is that David swears not to eat before sunset. He takes an oath: “May God punish me, and ever so severely, if I taste bread or anything else before the sun sets!” The people urged him to eat something while it was still day, friends. His answer was an oath.
The answer is False. The text says, “All the people took note and were pleased.” Everything the king did pleased them, friends. They weren't unhappy with how he handled Abner's death.

The word is convinced. The text says all the troops and all Israel “…were convinced that the king had no part in the murder of Abner…” Just before that, it says all the people took note and were pleased, friends. That's how the whole crowd came to be convinced.

The word is prince. David asks his servants, “Do you not realize that a great prince has fallen today in Israel?” That's the word he picks for Abner, friends. He's calling Abner great, even after all of this.

The answer is that David asks the LORD to repay the evildoer according to his evil. David ends with, “May the LORD repay the evildoer according to his evil!” Right before that, he says he's weak this day and the sons of Zeruiah are too fierce for him, friends. That request is the last thing he says in this passage.
